screenings.title: Brave New York
screenings.description: “BRAVE NEW YORK is a free-form documentary that loosely chronicles the last 12 years [as of 2004] of intense change in the East Village ‘hood.’ From the reopening of a newly curfewed Tompkins Square Park and Wigstock in ’92, to the destruction of the cherished Loisaida Community Gardens, to the yuppie invasions of the dot com years, to the present era, indelibly stamped with post 9/11 grief, this durable, lusty neighborhood survives in spite of a real estate gold rush that has excluded all but the well-to-do. The movie’s main voices are those of the artists and street people whose wisdom and commentaries upon the dominant culture give us pause amidst the speedy approach of a ‘Brave New World.’” –Richard SandlerCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Urban Video Project
screenings.description: “Urban Video Project (UVP) [was] a media education program [that ran] at Satellite Academy (Forsyth St.) from the mid-1980s through the 90s, providing students with the opportunity to craft half-hour documentaries as a cultural preservation effort, exploring the culture of Black and Latino people in their communities and the legacy of the African diaspora. Started by Salvatore LaSpada, a philanthropic consultant, Urban Video Project became integral to school culture at Satellite. It was emblematic of everything they were about: raising interest in learning and commitment to school through alternative pedagogy, hands-on, immersive experiences, one-on-one instruction, and allowing the students to be in control. […] The mission of these documentaries was twofold: to engage the students in school through media production, allowing them ‘to be the tellers of their stories,’ as LaSpada puts it, and to preserve the cultural heritage and current community of Black and Latino people in New York.” –Maddie DeLaere, XFR CollectiveThis program includes three tapes made by the students at the Lower East Side’s Satellite Academy as part of the Urban Video Project initiative, which have been preserved thanks to the efforts of the XFR Collective, Liz Andersen, and Salvatore LaSpada.NEW YORK, WEST INDIES: VOICES FROM THE JAMAICAN AND TRINIDADIAN MIGRATION 1986, 17 min, videoHigh school students of the Urban Video Project in New York City interview immigrants from Jamaica and Trinidad.EL PASAJE: RECOLLECTIONS FROM THE PUERTO RICAN MIGRATION 1986, 22.5 min, videoInterviewing the city’s Puerto Rican residents, the students learn about their history and the history of their classmates.EYES ON HARLEM 1987, 29 min, videoIn this tape, the students look at the community of Harlem in the mid 1980s as one of the legacies of the African Diaspora. They learn about present aspects of Harlem and the threat of hostile outside developers.Total running time: ca. 75 min.Introduced by Paige Laino (XFR Collective)!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bill Moyers Journal: Rosedale: the Way It Is
screenings.description: Amid the recession of the early 1970s, Black families began moving into nearly all-white Rosedale, a working-class Queens neighborhood just across the border from wealthy Nassau County. This film documents the explosive racist violence that followed: Tony and Glenda Spencer, a Black mother and father whose house was bombed twice but who refused to leave, anchor the film. “We’re going to stay here,” Glenda says. “Definitely going to stay.” (They did; as of 2019, she still lived in her home.) Moyers also follows a “home referral service” calling itself R.O.A.R. (Return Our American Rights) that aimed to keep Black people from becoming property owners in Rosedale, while moonlighting as a white supremacist terrorist gang. ROSEDALE was given a second life in 2019 when Sola Olosunde, a Hunter College graduate student in urban planning, sent out a viral tweet featuring the film’s most grotesque sequence, in which several Black children are assaulted by a group of white children. “Black and white alike in the Rosedales of America have been abandoned, condemned together to economic apartheid by a system that rewards the people who can afford to get out, and condemns to bitter, consuming rivalry those left behind,” Moyers opines. “It’s a travesty.”Introduced by photographer and public historian Sola Olosunde.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: À Tout Prendre
screenings.description: “A psychological drama depicting the birth and slow unraveling of a relationship within Montreal’s affluent bohemian circles. In this autobiographical debut feature – made in Quebec using cinéma direct methods and techniques – Claude Jutra reenacts his own romance with Johanne Harrelle. Set in the ‘open’ Montreal of the 1950s and 1960s, the film follows a young man trying to break into the film industry and a young Black woman – an orphan and a married woman – pursuing a modeling career. The two freely engage in a mutual confessional; this game of truth leads Johanne to question Claude about his probable homosexuality. They must also confront the agonizing dilemma of abortion when Johanne becomes pregnant. A slow unraveling of their relationship ensues.” –CINÉMATHÈQUE QUÉBÉCOISECLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Black Women’s Hands
screenings.description: This program surrounds JOJOLO with depictions of Black women artists. Sarah Maldoror’s TOTO BISSAINTHE (1984) chronicles her long-time friend and co-conspirator, the titular Haitian singer, in both the exteriority of performance and subjectivity of the backstage. HANDS OF INGE (1962) celebrates the sculptural craft of Ruth Inge Hardison and was edited by Hortense “Tee” Beveridge, the first Black woman to work as a unionized film editor. The 1962 documentary is among the rich constellation of citations in Simone Leigh and Madeleine Hunt-Ehrlich’s CONSPIRACY (2022), a spellbinding mediation on the artistry, manual skill, and aesthetic labor of Black women across forms.Lebert Bethune & John Taylor JOJOLO 1966, 22 min, 16mm. screenings.title: New Yorkers + Before the First Word
screenings.description: This program pairs two films, made a decade apart, that vividly demonstrate the vibrant, distinctive, and sometimes paradoxical nature of New York City’s neighborhoods: at once strikingly diverse and worldly, and yet close knit and self-enclosed. NEW YORKERS (1971), by filmmaker Michael Blackwood (who during his long career made several films about the city, as well as dozens of documentaries about artists, architects, and musicians), sets its sights on the Upper East Side, and in particular on the area in and around East 77th Street. BEFORE THE FIRST WORD (1982) – a co-production between WNET and the educational organization Learning Designs, and ostensibly a film designed as a teaching tool for journalism students – is set seventy-something blocks to the south, in Greenwich Village. Both films capture the degree to which their respective neighborhoods have developed specific cultures, institutions, and local networks to create a kind of shelter from the vertiginous, unceasing forces of change that animate Manhattan – and the degree to which they’re nevertheless unmistakably subject to the evolution that is the fate of all city neighborhoods, and to the more aggressive, inorganic tides of gentrification that have increasingly transformed the city over the past fifty years.Michael BlackwoodNEW YORKERS1971, 29 min, 16mm-to-DCPTom SimonBEFORE THE FIRST WORD1982, 29 min, videoTotal running time: ca. 60 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bouchra
screenings.description: With a lived-in granularity and unmistakable visual style, BOUCHRA, the feature debut from acclaimed visual artists Meriem Bennani and Orian Barki (best known together from their 2020 web series 2 LIZARDS), is a singular portrait effortlessly towing the line between documentary, visual art and resonant family drama. Deeply felt, surprisingly sexy and formally adventurous, Bennani and Barki’s distinctive debut forges new ground that “will make it a classic of queer cinema for years to come” (Next Best Picture).

screenings.title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
screenings.description: This film emerged from city planner William H. Whyte’s years of research into pedestrian behavior and city dynamics, conducted as part of his Street Life Project. His research resulted both in a film and a book, both of which closely analyzed the functioning of public spaces in various cities, above all in NYC. The book quickly became a classic text within the realm of city planning, and remains beloved not only for the wisdom and elegance of its insights, but for its disarmingly unpretentious, no-nonsense, and often flat-out funny tone. The film version fully embodies all the qualities of the book, and adds one special feature: Whyte’s own voice. Sounding very much like Jimmy Stewart’s city planner cousin, Whyte delivers the narration with an often-self-deprecatory folksiness that’s charmingly at odds with the stentorian tone of most educational films. The film is also effectively a work of street photography. Whyte and his team’s dedication to observing – and recording – the actual behavior of city dwellers, and their sharp eye for the behaviors and gestures that are most revealing of city life, result in a film that is – almost incidentally – a classic city symphony. THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES is one of the great films about that strangest of creatures – the city dweller – in its natural habitat.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: What Is the City but the People?
screenings.description: “In 1969 the Department of City Planning attempted to shore up support for its various [development] projects with a multipronged, multimedia public relations blitz. At its center was the publication of a six-volume book, ‘The Plan for New York City’ (1969), which articulated the commissioner’s vision for the metropolis to stem the flight of the middle classes to the suburbs and revitalize urban space. The plan was presented in synopsis form as a propagandistic documentary produced by the Department and co-directed by John Peer Nugent and Gordon Hyatt. Featuring some flashy cinematography from New York location shooter-extraordinaire Arthur J. Ornitz [THE CONNECTION; MINNIE & MOSKOWITZ; SERPICO], WHAT IS THE CITY is an idiosyncratic document of the city in the late 1960s, offering a wide panorama of places and spaces, narrated by one of the plan’s ghost writers, William H. Whyte [THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES]. The film flits between footage of and discussion about ‘urban crisis’ (uprisings, poor housing stock, street violence) and purported city-led remedies. Viewed today, the film is both a curious relic of failed urban policy and an index of just how wedded city authorities were (and remain) to the idea that the manipulation of public perception is key to urban governance.” –FILM AT LINCOLN CENTERCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Paradox on 72nd Street
screenings.description: Over the course of three years, Gene Searchinger filmed pedestrians, joggers, buskers, bench sitters, stoop sleepers, and countless other types of New Yorker (whom the narration describes as “exaggerated Americans”) at the corner of Broadway and 72nd St. Visually, the film presents an hour-long stream of individuals, each with their own unfathomable inner mindscape, who together comprise “the collective”; the paradox referred to in the title is narrator Lewis Thomas’s assertion that, “It is in our genes to live together and to depend on each other, to be our individual separate selves and at the same time the working parts of others.” Thomas, a biologist and the film’s co-writer, shares narrating duties with the anthropologist Philip Slater, both of whom offer meandering philosophical notes on individualism in American society.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Magician
screenings.description: Long though lost until its mysterious recovery in the late 20th century, Rex Ingram’s THE MAGICIAN remains one of Hollywood’s most extravagant explorations of the occult. It features Paul Wegener as the hypnotist Oliver Haddo (a character modeled on Aleister Crowley), who seeks out the blood of a virgin for his alchemical experiments in creating life. The film is based on W. Somerset Maugham’s 1908 novel of the same name, which Crowley vituperatively accused of plagiarism.Preceded by:Kenneth Anger INVOCATION OF MY DEMON BROTHER 1969, 12 min, 16mmTHE MAGICIAN will be shown alongside Kenneth Anger’s dense and mesmerizing INVOCATION OF MY DEMON BROTHER, which features the Moog drones of Mick Jagger and the Satanic presence of Anton LaVey. Anger held Ingram and his films in great esteem. He claimed that his grandmother, a wardrobe mistress, had worked on a number of his productions; through her stories of the time, the young Anger “became fascinated by this other period when nobody talked on the screen and when there were these magical, mythical images.”Total running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Brighton Beach
screenings.description: At once a charming portrait of the diverse residents of a unique New York City neighborhood, a vibrant time capsule of the city at the very beginning of the 1980s, and a penetrating exploration of the social and political dynamics of a rapidly changing community, BRIGHTON BEACH is a long-lost gem of documentary cinema that has been newly restored by IndieCollect. Directed with great empathy and perceptiveness by Carol Stein & Susan Wittenberg, BRIGHTON BEACH captures the Brooklyn neighborhood known as the poor man’s paradise – a city by the sea down the street from the Coney Island boardwalk. Interspersing interviews with the neighborhood’s residents – including the Soviet Jews who had begun arriving in large numbers at the time – with archival footage of the area fifty years earlier, the film is both a portrait of a very particular time and place as well as a study of the ways in which urban communities function, cohere, and continuously transform themselves.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

A cinematographic musing on contemporary Lebanon and a wager on the impossibility of recounting the violence of a bruised country, whose ghosts reappear from the ruins and stare at the screen, before disappearing in cross-fade.” –VISIONS DU RÉELGhassan SalhabNO TITLE2025, 42 min, DCP. It is not to reveal too much about NO TITLE to cite its closing statement, a gnomic endnote that hints at the unfathomably endless horrors of Israel’s war: ‘still today’.” –ALCHEMY FILM & ARTSTotal running time: ca. 75 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Leonora in the Morning Light + Q&A
screenings.description: In the early 1930s, painter Leonora Carrington, a rebel against social expectations, joins the surrealist movement and its iconic figures like André Breton and Salvador Dalí in Paris. A whirlwind love affair with artist Max Ernst confronts her with her inner demons. During the war, Leonora flees to Mexico and finally empowers herself. Today Leonora Carrington is one of the highest selling female painters worldwide, next to Frida Kahlo and Georgia O’Keeffe.

screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Terence Davies Trilogy
screenings.description: Terence Davies did not have a happy childhood, and his early adulthood was plagued by guilt and anguish over his homosexuality. But film became his outlet for self-expression, and in this trilogy of black-and-white short films, Davies brilliantly laid out the anguish of his bleak early years. In CHILDREN, Davies faces homophobic bullies at school and an abusive father at home. In MADONNA AND CHILD, the adult Davies spends his days visiting his aging mother, and his nights pursuing guilt-inducing sadomasochistic sex. DEATH AND TRANSFIGURATION allows Davies to imagine the circumstances of his twilight years and recall slightly fonder moments from his childhood. Though these brilliant films were underappreciated on their release, they announced Davies as a major talent who became one of the greatest gay filmmakers of all time. What better time could there be than the Christmas season to catch this unrelenting exploration of gay Catholic guilt and existential dread?“The trilogy did the rounds of the international festival circuits and was often seen – in the States in particular – as an unnecessarily pessimistic piece, receiving limited arthouse distribution as a result. In a ‘glad to be gay’ climate, the insecurity, guilt and downright loneliness so astutely expressed in these films was an unfashionable stance. Because Terence dared to show the pain of growing up Catholic and homosexual in working-class Liverpool in the ’50s and early ’60s, the films were not celebrated enough. Terence once told me that when he recognized his homosexuality he knelt in prayer for so long that his knees bled – this pain is conveyed in the spirit of his films.” –Jennifer Howarth, SIGHT AND SOUND, 1994CHILDREN (1976, 43 min, 16mm-to-DCP)MADONNA AND CHILD (1980, 30 min, 16mm-to-DCP)DEATH AND TRANSFIGURATION (1983, 23 min, 16mm-to-DCP)Total running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Ec: George Landow, Aka Owen Land
screenings.description: “The unique contribution of Land’s work lies in the fusion of intellectual reason and, significantly, the humor that distances it from the supposedly ‘boring’ world of avant-garde film. Having explored the basic properties of the celluloid strip itself in early works such as FILM IN WHICH THERE APPEAR…, his attention turned to the spectator in a series of ‘literal’ films that question the illusionary nature of cinema through the use of word play and visual ambiguity. His work often parodies experimental film itself by mimicking his contemporaries and mocking the solemn approach of film theorists and scholars.” –Mark Webber, TWO FILMS BY OWEN LANDFLEMING FALOON (1963, 6 min, 16mm)FILM IN WHICH THERE APPEAR EDGE LETTERING, SPROCKET HOLES, DIRT PARTICLES, ETC. screenings.title: Ec: Walden (diaries, Notes, and Sketches)
screenings.description: “Since 1950 I have been keeping a film diary. I have been walking around with my Bolex and reacting to the immediate reality: situations, friends, New York, seasons of the year. On some days I shot ten frames, on others ten seconds, still on others ten minutes. Or I shot nothing. When one writes diaries, it’s a retrospective process: you sit down, you look back at your day, and you write it all down. To keep a film (camera) diary, is to react (with your camera) immediately, now, this instant: either you get it now, or you don’t get it at all.” –Jonas MekasCLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!
